source: Zhu, Zhang, Luo (2022/2023) Biologically inspired design concept generation using generative pre-trained transformers
finding: Fine-tuned GPT-3 generators were built at three levels of problem looseness. The looser the problem space, the farther the generated bio-analogies sat from existing designs.
numbers: Word Mover's Distance on 3 AskNature robot samples, 50 concepts per sample per type (450 per type pooled). Type-1 (application only, loosest) was most diverse and close to the AskNature baseline; Type-3 (challenge statement, strictest) was least diverse.
limits: Distance measured by word2vec WMD, a proxy for far/near, not human-rated. One domain family (robotics). Fine-tuned Curie/Davinci era models.
agent_relevance: Loosening the problem statement before asking for analogies moves output from near to far. A scaffold can set analogical distance with a knob on how the problem is stated.

source: Zhu, Zhang, Luo (2022/2023) Biologically inspired design concept generation using generative pre-trained transformers
finding: Machine relevance filters and a small expert team showed the near/far trade: looser generators gave more novel but less feasible concepts.
numbers: Relevancy evaluators fine-tuned from Curie: 442 samples each (221 positive from AskNature, 221 negative), 4:1 train/validation split. Flying-car case, 50 concepts per type. Share passing evaluators (nature-solution / problem-solution / overall): Type-1 80% / n.a. / 80%; Type-2 80% / 58% / 50%; Type-3 66% / 84% / 62%. Over 50% of retrieved analogies were birds, then insects. Team of 10 engineers, 9 usable returns: Type-1 and 2 higher novelty, lower feasibility; Type-3 more feasible, less novel.
limits: Tiny human sample (9). Table layout for Type-2 read from PDF text and may be shifted. Birds-first retrieval echoes human attribute-similarity retrieval, so the model also shows the near bias.
agent_relevance: A code-side relevance classifier can screen far analogies, but expect it to be weakest at checking that the analogy actually solves the problem (58% vs 80%).

source: Ding, Srinivasan, MacNeil, Chan (2023) Fluid Transformers and Creative Analogies
finding: Prompt design changed how useful and how far GPT-3 cross-domain analogies were. One example beat zero examples.
numbers: text-davinci-002, temperature 1. Six design problems, 20 analogies each, across four prompt runs = 480 analogies. Judged potentially useful: one-shot 80% vs zero-shot 40%; few-shot 67%. Semantic similarity to the problem: one-shot below 0.5, zero-shot above 0.7, few-shot about 0.3. Best prompt gave 70% unique and useful.
limits: Judged by one researcher. Only one example set tested for one-shot. GPT-3 era model.
agent_relevance: Zero-shot analogy asks return near, restating answers. At least one worked example is needed to push the model out of the problem domain.

source: Ding, Srinivasan, MacNeil, Chan (2023) Fluid Transformers and Creative Analogies
finding: In a human task, LLM analogies were usually rated helpful for reformulating a design problem, mostly by adding information.
numbers: Prolific, 123 enrolled, N=110 finished, 220 analogy-response pairs. Median helpfulness 4/5. Coded responses: adding 185/220 (84.09%), rejecting 23/220 (10.45%). Second analogy rated 4 vs first rated 3 (Wilcoxon, p=0.002). 80% of tested analogies led to observable change in the formulation.
limits: No control condition without analogies. Single-session, lay participants, six problems.
agent_relevance: Analogies mostly extend a problem statement rather than overturn it. Expect elaboration, not reframing, from an analogy operator.

source: Ding, Srinivasan, MacNeil, Chan (2023) Fluid Transformers and Creative Analogies
finding: Researcher judgement of usefulness did not predict in-use helpfulness. Some outputs were flagged as harmful.
numbers: Point-biserial r = -0.0266, p = 0.6939 between a priori usable flag and helpfulness. Study 2: upper bound 25% outputs potentially harmful; five screeners flagged 1, 2, 2, 10 and 27 of 108 analogies; about 80% of harmful flags were upsetting content rather than bias or toxicity.
limits: Correlation used one researcher's ratings. Screener disagreement was large.
agent_relevance: Pre-screening analogies by an offline judge may not select the ones that help in use. Check usefulness by downstream effect, not by a rater.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) Beneath Surface Similarity: LLMs Make Reasonable Scientific Analogies after Structure Abduction
finding: Models do well on word analogies but much worse on structure-level system analogies (the Gentner mapping task).
numbers: SCAR benchmark: 400 scientific analogies across 13 fields. GPT-4 reached human level on most word-analogy sets but lagged on E-KAR. On SCAR English the first score column was GPT-4 73.28 (75.10 with background, 77.17 with 1-shot plus background) vs human 85.94. InstructGPT-002 51.18, ChatGPT 66.52. Small open models far lower (some near zero).
limits: Column headers lost in PDF extraction, so which metric the first column is cannot be confirmed. Humans were two graduate students.
agent_relevance: Word-analogy scores overstate structure mapping. Test any analogy operator on relational mapping, not on A:B::C:D.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) Beneath Surface Similarity: LLMs Make Reasonable Scientific Analogies after Structure Abduction
finding: Scaffolds changed results unevenly: chain of thought helped only the strongest model, and explanations beat generic step-by-step.
numbers: CoT with worked explanations raised GPT-4 but lowered ChatGPT and InstructGPT-003 (flawed reasoning). Explanation-CoT beat 'Let's think step by step'. Ten instruction templates: models were sensitive to wording, and an example, background or CoT reduced that sensitivity. GPT-4 accuracy varied by domain pair; similar domains such as biology and chemistry scored high; literature intra-domain was low. In an open setting (concepts not given) recall was low but precision was higher.
limits: Per-model effect sizes read from figures, not tables. Test on science analogies only.
agent_relevance: Do not turn on step-by-step analogy reasoning for weaker models. Near-field pairs are mapped more reliably than far pairs.

source: Bhavya, Xiong, Zhai (2022) Analogy Generation by Prompting LLMs: InstructGPT
finding: Share of meaningful generated analogies rose with model size; the largest matched humans only when no source was given.
numbers: Human evaluation, 1,407 analogies, 3 MTurk workers each, Fleiss kappa 0.347 on WSRC. % meaningful (0.3B / 1.3B / 6.7B / 175B / human): NO_SRC 1.90 / 15.61 / 48.29 / 70.05 / 66.67; WSRC (explain a given source) 8.97 / 29.05 / 38.46 / 53.79 / 71.88.
limits: High-school science only. Large models may have memorised textbook analogies. Fair agreement only.
agent_relevance: Free generation of a known analogy is easy for big models. Mapping to a specified distant source is harder; give the model the source domain when you want far analogies.

source: Bhavya, Xiong, Zhai (2022) Analogy Generation by Prompting LLMs: InstructGPT
finding: Prompt style, temperature and typos all moved analogy quality.
numbers: Best prompts were precise imperative statements at low temperature. Imperative beat question style. Low temperature (0) scored above temperature 0.85 on BLEURT overall; for example NO_SRC BLEURT 0.427 to 0.462 across prompts, WSRC 0.492 to 0.515. Spelling errors lowered scores. Study cost about $240.
limits: Automatic metric (BLEURT) with weak match to human judgement, as the authors say. High temperature only helped in a few cases.
agent_relevance: Higher temperature is not a reliable way to get farther analogies; change the prompt's source instruction instead.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Having the model recall its own related problems before solving (analogical prompting) beat zero-shot and few-shot chain of thought on math.
numbers: GSM8K, self-generated exemplars: GPT-3.5-turbo 77.8% (5-shot CoT 76.7%), text-davinci-003 61.0% (54.0%), PaLM2 81.7% (80.7%). MATH: GPT-3.5-turbo 37.3% (5-shot 34.9%), PaLM2 34.8% (34.3%). K=5 exemplars for GSM8K, K=3 for MATH.
limits: Gains are small on GSM8K (about 1 point over 5-shot). Mapping of table cells from PDF text. The recalled problems are near-field (same task type).
agent_relevance: Cheap, no retrieval store needed. It is a near-analogue method, so it should not be counted as evidence for far transfer.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Larger gains where problems need non-trivial algorithms; the method needs a strong enough model.
numbers: BIG-Bench (GPT-3.5-turbo, 0-shot / 0-shot CoT / 3-shot CoT / ours): word sorting 66.8 / 67.6 / 68.4 / 75.2; logical deduction 30.0 / 35.2 / 36.4 / 41.6; colored objects 50.4 / 61.6 / 62.0 / 68.0; formal fallacies 53.6 / 55.6 / 55.6 / 58.8; temporal sequences 40.4 / 44.8 / 58.0 / 57.6 (no gain). Codeforces: GPT-3.5 with self-generated knowledge plus exemplars 15% Acc@1 vs GPT-4 16%. On GSM8K, with small models (up to text-curie-001) retrieved exemplars beat self-generated ones.
limits: Single benchmark family per claim; no human comparison. Codeforces cells read from text.
agent_relevance: Use only when the model is large; at small scale retrieve real exemplars instead. Adding 'core concepts' before exemplars helped hard code tasks.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: On Gentner's story-analogy materials, GPT-3 handled near analogies but not far ones; humans handled both.
numbers: Humans N=54 UCLA undergraduates. Both preferred the causally matching target overall (GPT-3 binomial p=0.0005; humans t(53)=21.3). Near condition: GPT-3 p=0.0039, humans t(53)=21.5. Far condition: GPT-3 p=0.065 (not significant), humans t(53)=16.7. Humans beat GPT-3 (OR=0.37, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.63, p=0.0003). 15 of 54 humans chose the analogous story every trial. GPT-4 preliminary: stronger, near perfect on near, better on far.
limits: GPT-4 test was preliminary and in the supplement. Later work (c16) showed answer-order and paraphrase effects.
agent_relevance: This is the clean machine version of the near/far split: near is solved, far is where models and scaffolds are weak.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 reproduced the classic Gick and Holyoak need-a-cue pattern for analogical problem solving.
numbers: Radiation problem alone: GPT-3 proposed injecting a source into the tumour. After the general story: found the convergence solution and explained the mapping (general to doctor, dictator to tumour, army to rays). With two distractor stories added: no convergence solution until prompted to consider the earlier stories, then it picked the general story and solved it. On the children's gumball-transfer task it gave mechanically nonsensical elaborate solutions.
limits: Qualitative, one model, a few cases. The source was supplied in context, so retrieval was not tested.
agent_relevance: The failure is retrieval from distractors, not mapping. An explicit 'which earlier case is relevant' step recovers it.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat humans on most non-story analogy tests, and showed a human-like semantic distance effect on verbal analogies.
numbers: Digit Matrices (Raven-style text): GPT-3 matched or exceeded humans in most settings; SPM comparison data N=80. Letter strings: humans N=57. UCLA Verbal Analogy Test: humans N=57; GPT-3 as good or better. SAT analogies: above average high-school level. Jones et al. set: humans did worse when analogs were semantically distant, as did GPT-3.
limits: Training data may contain the letter-string and verbal items; see c15 for counterfactual tests.
agent_relevance: Distance cost appears in models too, so far-source analogy needs help in any scaffold.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: On letter-string analogies with altered alphabets, humans stayed high and GPT models fell sharply.
numbers: Humans N=136 on Prolific. Mean accuracy over counterfactual alphabets: humans 0.753 [0.734, 0.773], GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452. Human accuracy stayed flat as more letters were permuted. Error types differ: GPT-4 more often used an alternative rule.
limits: Letter-strings are not design analogies. Comprehension checks showed the models understood the permuted alphabets.
agent_relevance: Successes on familiar analogy forms may be retrieval. An agent should verify transfer on a changed surface form.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Webb's story-analogy result is fragile: answer order and paraphrasing change GPT-4 scores.
numbers: 18 far-analogy story problems. GPT-4 (Webb) correct-first 0.89 (16/18), correct-second 0.61 (11/18), total 0.75. GPT-4 (their run) 1.0 (18/18), 0.72 (13/18), total 0.86 (31/36). Humans N=720 presentations: 0.78 first, 0.78 second. Paraphrasing the correct answer: GPT-4 0.86 down to 0.72 (26/36); human accuracy also dropped. Digit matrices: brittle on one of two variants. Letter strings: drops for GPT models, not humans.
limits: Only 18 items, so intervals are wide. Their text notes humans are also helped by surface overlap.
agent_relevance: A weakened replication of the strong 'emergent analogy' claim. Randomise order and paraphrase candidate sources in any analogy test.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy
finding: Story-level analogy identification is hard for LLMs, especially when distractors share entities with the source.
numbers: 24K story pairs annotated on entity similarity and relation similarity (0 to 3). Multiple choice: random 25%, humans 85.7%; ChatGPT about 30%, GPT-3.5 37.1%, LLaMa-65B 28.6%, FlanT5-xxl 45.4%. Best model 37.7 points below humans. Models picked easy random negatives under 20% of the time but were drawn to hard negatives that shared nouns. Fine-tuned FlanT5-xxl matched zero-shot ChatGPT on generated-analogy quality.
limits: Generation quality scored by crowd workers on 40 source stories. Dataset built partly with LLMs.
agent_relevance: Surface-matching distractors defeat models: the same trap as near-field fixation in people.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: Zero-shot LLMs recognise near analogies but fail far ones; GPT-4 was below chance on the hardest far-versus-near pairing.
numbers: 1,096 triples (294 far-disanalogy and 254 near-disanalogy pairs). GPT-4 zero-shot with explicit system-mapping instruction: 94.0, 92.5 on the two near-analogy partitions; 57.1 and 29.1 on the two far-analogy partitions (chance 50). GPT-3.5: 88.1, 81.3, 50.4, 21.7. Without the instruction GPT-4's last cell was 17.7.
limits: Column order read from the paper's near/far description, not the header, which the PDF text dropped. Narratives are short proverb stories.
agent_relevance: The far-analogy failure is reproduced on a second benchmark with a different method. Do not trust an unaided model to judge far analogies.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: Demonstrations helped far-analogy detection but hurt near-analogy detection; far demonstrations and CoT worked best.
numbers: With 0, 2, 4, 6 solved demonstrations: both near and far demonstrations improved far-analogy detection and were detrimental on near; more far demonstrations gradually improved near detection too. CoT demonstrations (extract the proverb message, then predict) helped more than plain demonstrations. Best model in the few-shot setting was only halfway between random and humans.
limits: Near/far demonstration split run on GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 only (GPT-4 cost). Effects read from figures.
agent_relevance: Demonstrations teach the model to ignore surface overlap. Show far cases, not near ones, and ask for the abstract message first.

source: Yu and He (2024) Thought Propagation: An Analogical Approach to Complex Reasoning with LLMs (ICLR)
finding: An LLM-agent loop that solves analogous problems first and reuses their solutions beat solving from scratch.
numbers: Three tasks. Average +12% absolute in finding the optimal solution on shortest-path reasoning; +13% human preference on creative writing; +15% task completion on LLM-agent planning (household text-game). Method: propose analogous problems, solve each, aggregate to refine or plan the input problem.
limits: Analogous problems are near-field neighbours (same task type, nearby graph or goal). Numbers are from the abstract. Extra calls per item, so cost is higher.
agent_relevance: A working example of analogy inside an agent loop. Close enough to O7 to copy the shape: propose, solve, transfer, then check with a code verifier.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur, Shahaf (2017) Accelerating Innovation Through Analogy Mining (KDD)
finding: Retrieving by purpose and mechanism, not surface words, raised the chance people produced good ideas. Inspirations were more distant than keyword matches.
numbers: 38 AMT workers, 12 seed products, within-subjects, 749 ideas. Majority-vote 'good': 184 ideas. Share good: analogy-mining 38% (N=118), random 22% (68), TF-IDF 21% (63), p<.01. Mixed model pr(good): k=3 0.56 [0.36, 0.75] vs TF-IDF 0.16, random 0.14; k=2 0.71 vs 0.28 and 0.27. Likelihood ratio chi2(3)=92.38 for k=3. Test pairs N=2,500 with about 5,500 products for training. Workers needed a scaffold (write a schema, then a more abstract one) to avoid surface matches. TF-IDF returned same-domain items.
limits: Wide confidence intervals as the authors note. Judged by five graduate students. Crowd, not professional designers. Seeds were everyday products.
agent_relevance: Retrieve by abstract function (purpose plus mechanism), not by keywords. This is the older computational system closest to a far-analogy retriever.

source: Zhu and Luo (2022) Generative Transformers for Design Concept Generation
finding: Domain-specialised GPT models given near or far patent fields produced different novelty, but the pattern faded for few-shot GPT-3.
numbers: Rolling-toy concepts, 6 reference domains ranked by knowledge distance (13th, 17th, 28th nearest vs 64th, 68th, 100th). GPT-2 355M fine-tuned per domain, 20,000 steps, 500 concepts each. Unique ideas: Weapons 35.8% (179/500), Agriculture 40.8% (204/500) for GPT-2; GPT-3 few-shot (10 sampled titles) 71.8% and 67.4%. TechNet term relevance: far-field models scored lower (more novel) than near-field; pattern far less obvious for GPT-3 few-shot. Far-field concept descriptions were longer.
limits: Novelty proxy confounded with text length, as the authors note. No feasibility rating. Single design topic.
agent_relevance: Prompt-only agents get weaker domain specialisation than fine-tuned ones, so the far-field effect may need real retrieved source text.

source: Luo, Sarica, Wood (2021) Guiding data-driven design ideation by knowledge distance
finding: A patent-class network estimates knowledge distance between fields to steer near or far stimuli for designers.
numbers: Network of all technology fields in patent classification; two case studies (rolling toy and an open-ended innovation case). Authors expect farther sources to give more novel but less feasible ideas.
limits: No controlled test. Case demonstrations only. Distance is statistical co-occurrence of patent classes.
agent_relevance: A computed distance measure plus a chosen band lets code, not the model, choose between near and far sources.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?
finding: Blind expert review found LLM ideas more novel than expert ideas, but this is generation in general, not analogy specifically.
numbers: 79 expert reviewers, 49 ideas per condition, nearly 300 reviews. Novelty: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI reranked by human 5.81 (AI vs human p<0.05, multiple-test corrected).
limits: Not an analogy study. Feasibility did not favour AI ideas in the authors' summary; treat other claims about diversity as unchecked here.
agent_relevance: Novelty of model output is not a sign that distant analogy occurred. Measure distance directly.

source: Li, Zhang, Cao, Chen (2026) Beyond Input-Output: Rethinking Creativity through Design-by-Analogy in Human-AI Collaboration (CHI 26)
finding: Systematic review of 85 studies on AI-driven design by analogy. It finds little rigorous testing of AI analogy outputs.
numbers: 85 studies; six representation forms; seven creative-process stages. Analogy-making split into four computational stages: representation, retrieval, mapping, evaluation. Authors state there is a significant lack of rigorous empirical evaluation of novelty, feasibility and utility in AI-driven DbA. Proposes AI as candidate generator and humans as filters.
limits: Review, so no new measurements. The homogenisation risk from foundation models is asserted, not quantified here.
agent_relevance: Supports building O7 with a verify step. The four-stage split (represent, retrieve, map, evaluate) is a usable operator design.

source: Gentner and Markman (1997) Structure Mapping in Analogy and Similarity
finding: Founding model for machine analogy: the Structure-Mapping Engine aligns relational structure in three stages. Retrieval follows surface similarity but problem-solving success follows structural match.
numbers: SME stages: local match hypotheses, merge into structurally consistent kernels, merge kernels into one or a few maximal interpretations; returns two or three best interpretations; can extend a mapping incrementally. Cites MAC/FAC (Forbus, Gentner, Law 1995) as the retrieval model.
limits: Theory paper, older. No SME performance numbers were taken from it.
agent_relevance: Explains why LLMs fail far analogies: retrieval sides with surface features. A separate relational check (map, then verify) matches this architecture.
